title: Online presence: community groups, profiles and consent-based content
audience: Solo operators and team owners in any service business who want local customers to find them online and trust them, without breaking group rules or consent requirements.
learningOutcomes: Read a community group's rules and write a helpful answer or post that complies with them.
Prepare a before-and-after or completed-work post from a finished job, with written consent and identifying details removed.
Set up an opt-in email list and state the sender identity and unsubscribe approach before the first send.

instruction.heading: Join the groups where your customers already ask questions
instruction.body: Local neighbourhood groups, parents' groups, strata and body corporate owner groups, and pet owner or garden communities are where future customers ask for help. Join the groups that match your service area, not only groups for other tradespeople. Before you post anything, read the group rules, including whether business posts, offers and direct messages are allowed. Answer questions with specific, practical help, such as how to tell whether a piece of equipment needs servicing or when a routine task is due, and mention your business only where the rules and the question allow it. Do not message members first to offer your service unless the group rules and the member have clearly allowed it. ACMA's guidance says marketing messages need consent, so check whether a direct message counts as a commercial message before you send one.

instruction.heading: Keep the profile customers find accurate
instruction.body: When someone searches for your service in your area, your online business listing is often the first thing they see. Keep the business name, service area, service list, hours and contact method accurate and current. Add photos of completed work only when the customer has agreed to that use, and never use photos from other businesses without their permission. Reply to every enquiry within a time you state on the listing, and say so if you cannot respond out of hours. An accurate, responsive listing also makes it easier to ask for reviews later, because customers who want to thank you will find it.

instruction.heading: Share completed work with consent and no identifying details
instruction.body: Before-and-after photos, or photos of any finished job, show results clearly, but they can expose a customer's home or site, routine and identity. Ask for written consent before you post, and say where the photo will appear. Before posting, crop or blur the street number, street sign, number plates, faces, children, pets and personal items, and remove location data from the file. Do not name the customer or describe the property or site in a way that identifies them. Cropping is part of the preparation, not a replacement for consent. If the customer withdraws consent, remove the post and any copies you control, and record the date.

instruction.heading: Post useful seasonal tips on a schedule you can keep
instruction.body: A small number of practical tips, posted regularly, builds more trust than frequent promotion. Choose one platform first, and plan a simple calendar tied to local conditions, such as an opening or closing checklist, a maintenance check before the wet season, care advice during hot weather, or a spring clean-up. Write each post as a short, practical instruction a customer could use that day, and end with one optional next step. Keep the posts that get answers, and drop the formats that do not. Post no more often than you can answer the replies.

instruction.heading: Build an opt-in email list for people who asked to hear from you
instruction.body: An email list lets you contact people who chose to hear from you again. Offer a useful resource, such as a seasonal checklist, in exchange for an email address, and make the sign-up a clear, separate choice that is not pre-ticked. The sign-up should say what you will send and how often. Every commercial message must identify you as the sender and include a working way to unsubscribe, and you should act on each unsubscribe within five working days at the latest, and sooner where you can. The rules come from the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA's avoid-spam guidance (read 2026-11-03) summarises them: the sender must be identified accurately, and the unsubscribe option must be free, work for at least 30 days and be honoured within five working days. “Finding your first customers through direct, consent-based outreach” covers consent and spam rules in more detail.

procedure: Identify two or three groups in your service area and read each group's rules.
Answer one real question in a group, within its rules, and record the response.
Check the online business listing for accuracy and set a response time.
Obtain written consent for one completed job, then prepare the photo by cropping and removing identifying details.
Plan four weeks of seasonal tips for one platform, with one optional next step in each post.
Draft the opt-in sign-up wording, the sender identification and the unsubscribe step, and check them against current ACMA guidance before launch.
Remove any post or contact whose consent or unsubscribe request has been withdrawn, and record the date.

workedExamples.situation: A service operator finishes a job at a family's home and wants to post the result in a community group and on the business listing. The family has not replied to the request for permission, and the photo shows the street-facing fence and the house number on the gate.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can the post go up, and what should the operator do instead?
workedExamples.reasoning: It cannot go up yet. Without written consent the post is not allowed, and the fence and gate number would identify the home even if consent arrived later. The operator follows up once with the family. If there is still no reply, the operator posts a photo from a different job where the customer has agreed, or a close-up of the tools used on the job with a seasonal tip. The operator posts to the community group only if the group's rules allow business posts.

equipmentAndPpe: List of community groups with the rules recorded for each
Consent form or written consent message for photos and reviews
Photo editing tool that can crop, blur and remove location data
Seasonal content calendar for one platform
Opt-in sign-up wording checked against current ACMA guidance
No PPE is needed for online work

commonErrors.error: Posting an offer in a group whose rules do not allow it.
commonErrors.prevention: Read the group rules before every post and answer questions instead of advertising where promotion is not allowed.

commonErrors.error: Publishing a customer photo after only cropping it, without written consent.
commonErrors.prevention: Obtain written consent first, then crop and remove identifying details.

commonErrors.error: Adding people to an email list who did not choose to join.
commonErrors.prevention: Use a separate, unticked opt-in, and send only what the person signed up for.

commonErrors.error: Advertising licensed work the business is not licensed to do.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the licence for each service before it appears on the listing or in a post.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Community groups can remove posts and members who break their rules. Read the rules before each post, and do not treat silence from a group as permission.

Client photos and details should have written consent before they are published, and blurring or cropping does not replace that consent. If the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) applies to your business, publishing identifiable client information is also a privacy matter. The OAIC's small business guidance (summary read 2026-11-03) says small businesses with annual turnover of $3 million or less are generally exempt, with some exceptions, so check whether the Act applies to you.

Commercial electronic messages, including email, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA's avoid-spam guidance (read 2026-11-03) says consent is required before marketing messages and should be recorded, and that inferred consent is less reliable than express consent. The Act text was not read for this lesson, so confirm it and current ACMA guidance before sending.

Do not advertise licensed or authorised work that you do not hold the licence for in the state or territory where the work is done, such as electrical, gas or other restricted work. Check the rule in each state or territory you work in.

qualityStandard: Every group post or reply follows the written rules of that group.
Every published photo has written consent on file and no identifying details visible.
Every email list member has opted in, and every unsubscribe is actioned promptly.
documentationEvidence: Group rules record with the date each was checked.
Written consent record for each published photo, with a withdrawal log.
Opt-in record for each email list member, and the unsubscribe log.
summary: Be useful in the groups your customers use, and follow each group's rules.
Publish customer work only with written consent and with identifying details removed.
Email only people who opted in, identify yourself as the sender, and honour every unsubscribe.

knowledgeChecks.question: A neighbourhood group does not allow business posts. What should you do?
options: Post your offer anyway, because it is helpful to members and members will like it
Answer questions where you can help, and follow the group's rules on promotion
Message every member privately with your price list and ask them to call you

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you post a photo of a finished job, what must you have?
options: The customer's written consent, with identifying details cropped or blurred
Only the belief that the photo looks professional and the photo is kept for the file
A promise from the customer that they will share it themselves

knowledgeChecks.question: Under the approach in this lesson, what must a commercial email to a list include?
options: A discount code, a picture of the product and a link to the shop, with no other details
A long list of past reviews and nothing else, with no name or contact details
Identification of you as the sender and a working way to unsubscribe, checked against current ACMA guidance

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam
officialReferences.covers: ACMA guidance on the Spam Act 2003: consent is required before marketing messages, and keeping a record of express consent is advised; inferred consent is less reliable than express consent; the sender must be identified accurately with correct contact details kept for at least 30 days; every commercial message must contain an unsubscribe option that is clear, free, needs no account or extra personal information, and works for at least 30 days; unsubscribe requests must be honoured within 5 working days. Publisher: Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA). This is a summary of the guidance, not the Act text, which was not read.
